reference.source: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology / neuromuscular disease literature
clinicalPearls: The commonest acquired myopathy after middle age, affecting men more often than women
Characteristic pattern of weakness targets the finger flexors and the quadriceps, often asymmetrically
Early falls from knee buckling and difficulty with grip and fine hand tasks are typical presentations
Dysphagia is common and can be an early or dominant feature
Creatine kinase is normal or only mildly raised, unlike in other inflammatory myopathies
Muscle biopsy shows rimmed vacuoles, endomysial inflammation, and protein aggregates such as those staining for p62 and TDP-43
Unlike polymyositis and dermatomyositis, it is largely resistant to corticosteroids and immunosuppression
reference.pathophysiology: Sporadic inclusion body myositis is a slowly progressive myopathy with combined inflammatory and degenerative features. Endomysial T-cell infiltration and up-regulation of major histocompatibility complex on muscle fibres coexist with a degenerative process marked by rimmed vacuoles and intracellular accumulation of misfolded proteins, including beta-amyloid, phosphorylated tau, TDP-43, and p62. The relative contribution of autoimmunity and protein mishandling remains debated, but the degenerative component is thought to explain the characteristic treatment resistance and the selective, progressive involvement of finger flexors and quadriceps.
additionalDifferentials: Motor neurone disease and other anterior horn cell disorders
Myasthenia gravis with limb and bulbar weakness
additionalInvestigations: Muscle biopsy showing rimmed vacuoles, endomysial inflammation, and characteristic protein aggregates
Creatine kinase measurement, typically normal or only mildly elevated
Electromyography showing a mixed myopathic and occasionally neurogenic pattern
Anti-cN1A (NT5C1A) antibody testing as a supportive marker
Swallowing assessment given the frequency of dysphagia
redFlags: Rapid functional decline suggesting an alternative diagnosis
Marked weight loss or bulbar deterioration
reference.prognosis: The condition progresses slowly but relentlessly over years, leading to significant disability, dependence on mobility aids, and swallowing difficulties; life expectancy is relatively preserved but quality of life declines with functional loss.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as treatment-resistant polymyositis and prolonging futile immunosuppression
Being reassured by a normal creatine kinase into excluding a myopathy
Overlooking the diagnostic finger-flexor and quadriceps weakness pattern
Failing to recognise and manage dysphagia and aspiration risk
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Recognition that no immunotherapy reliably alters the course, so prolonged immunosuppression is generally avoided
Physiotherapy with a tailored aerobic and resistance exercise programme to maintain strength and function
Occupational therapy, mobility aids, ankle-foot orthoses and falls-prevention measures for weakness of the quadriceps and finger flexors
Speech and language therapy for dysphagia, with dietary modification and consideration of cricopharyngeal dilatation, myotomy or botulinum toxin for troublesome swallowing
Monitoring of swallowing and respiratory function to anticipate aspiration and nutritional compromise
Multidisciplinary neuromuscular follow-up with support for progressive disability and advance care planning
